fixes.explanation: Egypt it is, friend. The LORD says, "When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son." (Hosea 11:1) Notice that the love and the calling sit side by side in this one verse. That's a good thing to hold onto before the rest of this chapter gets rough.

Babylon is a big name in the Bible, so I get why it jumped out. But here the LORD says, "…out of Egypt I called My son." (Hosea 11:1) Babylon never comes up in these verses. Egypt is the place He called His son out of.
Moab might have crossed your mind, and that's fair. But the LORD says, "…out of Egypt I called My son." (Hosea 11:1) Moab isn't in this passage at all. Egypt is the place He called His son out of.

False, and the text is blunt about it. "But the more I called Israel, the farther they departed from Me." (Hosea 11:2) The more He called, the farther they went. I think that must have been a hard thing for a loving Father to watch.

The Baals, that's right. Hosea 11:2 says, "They sacrificed to the Baals and burned incense to carved images." Baals were false gods, and the text puts them right next to carved images. Israel was walking away from the LORD while sacrificing to the Baals.

Molech does show up elsewhere in Scripture (Leviticus 18:21), so I see why it came to mind. But this verse names a different one: "They sacrificed to the Baals and burned incense to carved images." (Hosea 11:2) Molech isn't mentioned here. The Baals are the answer.

Dagon was a god of the Philistines (Judges 16:23), so I see why it came to mind. But Hosea 11:2 says, "They sacrificed to the Baals and burned incense to carved images." Dagon never shows up in these verses. It's the Baals this time.

False, and that stings a little. "…they never realized that it was I who healed them." (Hosea 11:3) The LORD took Ephraim by the arms and taught them to walk, and they never realized it was He who healed them. I think that's the kind of thing a dad remembers.

Count isn't in this verse, friend. Hosea 11:4 says, "I lifted the yoke from their necks and bent down to feed them." The yoke comes off and He bends down to feed them. Nothing in it is about counting. It's all care.

That's the reason the text gives, baker. "Will they not return to the land of Egypt and be ruled by Assyria because they refused to repent?" (Hosea 11:5) Assyria is the one named to rule them. The reason is the refusing, nothing else.

That's the one, friend! After all of that, the LORD asks, "How could I give you up, O Ephraim?" (Hosea 11:8) Then the next line asks, "How could I surrender you, O Israel?" Right after the hard warnings comes a question full of love.

That's what you might expect after all those warnings. But the LORD says, "How could I give you up, O Ephraim?" (Hosea 11:8) He doesn't ask why He should keep Ephraim. He asks how He could give Ephraim up.

Jealousy shows up in other places in Scripture, like Exodus 34:14, but not in this verse. Here the LORD says, "My heart is turned within Me; My compassion is stirred!" (Hosea 11:8) Compassion is what's stirring in Him.

It's a natural guess, since the prophet Amos pleads for Jacob in Amos 7:2. But in this passage nobody begs Him. The LORD says, "For I am God and not man—the Holy One among you—and I will not come in wrath." (Hosea 11:9) That's His own reason, in His own words.
A bear can sure growl, I'll give you that. But the text says, "He will roar like a lion." (Hosea 11:10) The LORD's roar is compared to a lion's, not a bear's.

False, friend. "When He roars, His children will come trembling from the west." (Hosea 11:10) They come trembling, and the text never has them running away. I think those must be some shaky steps, but they are steps in the right direction.
